mcqs.question: Why do large-scale recommenders split into candidate generation and ranking instead of scoring the whole catalog for every user?
options: Because implicit feedback only works on a small number of items at a time
Because ranking models can't process more than a few hundred items in their training data
Because scoring every item for every user is computationally infeasible at millions-of-items scale, so a cheap stage first narrows to a plausible subset
Because collaborative filtering requires items to be pre-sorted alphabetically before scoring
mcqs.explanation: The two-stage split exists purely for compute cost: a cheap, coarse retrieval stage cuts millions of items down to hundreds, and only those get the expensive, precise ranking model. Ranking models have no inherent item-count limit (wrong distractor), and neither implicit feedback nor sort order is the reason for the split.

mcqs.question: A brand-new item just got uploaded with zero interactions. Which approach can still recommend it, and why?
options: Collaborative filtering, because it recomputes user similarity in real time
Collaborative filtering, because popularity signals bootstrap new items automatically
Neither approach can recommend a zero-interaction item until it accumulates clicks
Content-based filtering, because it can match the item's own features (tags, description) to a user's history without needing any interaction data on the item itself
mcqs.explanation: Content-based filtering only needs the item's own features, so a new item is scorable the moment it exists. Collaborative filtering needs interaction data to place an item near others in latent space — with zero interactions it has literally no signal, regardless of how 'real-time' the similarity computation is.

mcqs.question: A user likes 8 items total in the catalog, and a recommender's top-5 list contains 3 of them. What are precision@5 and recall@5?
options: Precision@5 and recall@5 are both always equal to each other by definition
mcqs.explanation: Precision@5 asks what fraction of the 5 shown items were relevant (3/5 = 0.6), while recall@5 asks what fraction of all 8 relevant items were captured in the top 5 (3/8 = 0.375) — they measure different things and are generally not equal. The other options invert or misapply the denominators.

mcqs.question: A recommender achieves excellent RMSE predicting exact star ratings. Why might it still produce a mediocre top-5 recommendation list for users?
options: RMSE and top-k list quality are mathematically identical, so this cannot happen

RMSE rewards accuracy across the entire ratings range, not specifically getting the relative order of the highest-rated items correct — a model can have low RMSE while still misordering exactly the top items users actually see
RMSE can only be computed for classification tasks, not rating prediction
This only happens if the model was trained on too little data
mcqs.explanation: RMSE is a global error measure across all predictions, not a ranking-aware metric focused on the top of the list — a model can be accurate on average while still getting the fine-grained ordering among top candidates wrong, which is exactly what users experience. RMSE and top-k quality are related but not identical, RMSE is precisely a rating-prediction (regression-style) metric, and this mismatch isn't specifically a data-quantity problem.
